Studies of knowledge conflicts have examined how language models respond when prompts contain information that differs from their stored knowledge. These investigations suggest that models may follow contextual information even when it is misleading, while in other cases they may disregard valid evidence because of strong parametric priors. The outcome can depend on factors such as the position, salience, phrasing, and apparent credibility of the context. Such findings motivate methods that explicitly model the reliability of retrieved information rather than treating all context tokens as equally trustworthy.

Sociolinguistic research has long shown that dialects are evaluated not only as linguistic varieties but also as signals of social identity, regional belonging, and group membership. Although dialect use is often associated with solidarity and authenticity within local communities, speakers may also be judged through stereotypes concerning intelligence, competence, education, trustworthiness, or social status. These evaluations can vary according to the listener, the social context, and the perceived prestige of the dialect. Standard-language varieties are frequently treated as more appropriate in institutional and formal settings, while regional varieties may be framed as informal, less prestigious, or less suitable for professional communication. Work on German language attitudes similarly documents the coexistence of regional pride and negative judgments toward speakers of particular dialects. This literature motivates examining dialect bias as a multidimensional phenomenon rather than assuming that all regional varieties receive the same social evaluation.

Humans often address complex problems by recognizing recurring structures in examples. Rather than memorizing each solution verbatim, they may identify abstract components—such as a narrative transition, a proof strategy, or an intermediate reasoning step—and recombine these components in a new context. This suggests a broader role for foundation models: beyond generating text directly, they may be used to infer latent structures from collections of documents and to guide generation through those structures. The challenge is to obtain representations that are sufficiently abstract to generalize across documents, while retaining enough information to reconstruct the content and functions of individual segments.

A multi-agent system with hidden participants can be viewed as a particularly challenging partial-knowledge environment. The attacker may know the architecture or behavior of one agent while lacking direct access to the other agents, their prompts, their roles, and their decision rules. In addition, the attacker must account for the possibility that the target agent will be challenged, corrected, or outweighed during collaboration. Thus, optimizing solely for the response of the known agent may not produce a successful collective attack. This motivates approaches that model possible interactions with unknown agents rather than treating the target agent as an isolated predictor.
